Sources and chapter boundaries

This chapter develops algorithm correctness, from state-based specifications to complete proofs of searching, sorting, arithmetic and certificate verification. Read the earlier chapters on induction, logical implication, loop invariants and divide and conquer when a prerequisite needs reinforcement. Here, every proof connects to an executable algorithm or a precise mathematical question. Correctness, termination, safety and efficiency are separate claims, and every algorithm states which claims are established.

Contracts, states and the meaning of correctness

A state gives values to variables and identifies the current control location. For arrays, it also gives each indexed value; for mutable objects, it records shared references. A program command maps an initial state to an execution that may terminate normally, fail, or continue indefinitely. A mathematical pseudocode model uses exact integers unless a finite arithmetic model is explicitly declared.

A precondition P describes the admitted initial states. A postcondition Q describes the required final state. The notation {P}C{Q} here means partial correctness: every normally terminating execution from a state satisfying P ends in a state satisfying Q. It says nothing about a nonterminating execution. We establish safety separately, so the absence of normal termination through an error cannot count as a useful correctness certificate. Total correctness means partial correctness together with termination for every admitted input; our complete algorithm claims also require safe evaluation of every expression and array access.

For a sorting routine, “the result is sorted” is an incomplete contract. A routine returning an empty array satisfies that sentence for every input. Let A0 be an immutable snapshot of the initial array, and let bag(A) denote its multiset of values, including multiplicities. A complete value-level contract is:

bag(A)=bag(A0)

For every valid adjacent index, meaning 0≤i<n-1, require:

A[i]≤A[i+1].

The quantified set is empty when the array has fewer than two elements. Stability is an additional contract: equal-key records retain their original relative order. If the procedure sorts in place, its frame condition must also specify which memory it may modify. Correctness of a sorted list of keys does not establish correctness of record identities, payloads or external aliases.

Specifications can be inconsistent or too weak. An impossible precondition makes a partial-correctness triple vacuously valid. A postcondition that merely says “the output is an integer” does not specify exponentiation. Before proving anything, identify the input domain, mathematical function, permitted mutation, empty-input convention and tie rule.

Example: two meanings of exponentiation. Over exact integers, the result of input (3,6) is 729. Under arithmetic modulo 256, the corresponding residue is 217. A proof of one result does not prove the other. Unsigned finite-width arithmetic, signed arithmetic and arbitrary-precision arithmetic must not be interchanged silently. In C, unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo its range; signed overflow is not defined as ordinary modular wrapping.

Backward reasoning and verification conditions

Suppose a pure assignment is x = E, and the expression is defined in every admitted state. To establish a desired postcondition Q, substitute the old expression E for every free occurrence of the assigned variable in Q. This is substitution in the logical formula, not substitution of a newly computed value into the old expression. Bound variables must be renamed if necessary to avoid capture.

wp(x:=E,Q)=Q[E/x].

For example, after x = x + 3, the requirement x2=25 becomes (x+3)2=25, hence old x=-8 or old x=2. A forward guess such as x=5 refers to the final state and is not the required initial condition. Over fixed-width arithmetic, this algebra must be repeated in the specified arithmetic model and include any safety obligation.

For a sequence, reason backward from the final command first:

wp(C1;C2,Q)=wp(C1,wp(C2,Q)).

For x = x + 1; y = 2*x, and final requirement y=10, the second assignment requires 2x=10, so the first requires 2(x+1)=10, giving initial x=4. Initial y is irrelevant because it is overwritten. Reversing the substitution order gives the wrong state relationship.

For a total, pure Boolean guard B:

Write the two guarded requirements separately:

F1=(B⇒wp(C1,Q)),
F2=(¬B⇒wp(C2,Q)).

The conditional's weakest precondition is their conjunction F1∧F2.

The guard is evaluated in the initial state of the conditional. For if x < 0: x = -x, the omitted else branch is skip. Thus x≥0 afterward follows both when initial x<0 and when initial x≥0. In machine signed integers, negating the minimum representable value requires separate analysis; the exact-integer proof alone does not justify the implementation.

The consequence rule permits a stronger precondition and a weaker postcondition. If P'⇒P, the known triple {P}C{Q} applies to P'; if Q⇒Q', its result implies Q'. The directions matter. Proving correctness for positive inputs does not prove it for all integers. Proving the exact result does imply a looser result bound, but a loose bound does not identify the exact result.

An array update must account for aliasing of indices. For A[i] = v, model the new array as a functional update: its value at j is v when j=i, and old A[j] otherwise. In A[i]=1; A[j]=2, the desired postcondition A[i]=1∧A[j]=2 requires i≠j, assuming both indices are valid. Treating the two indexed cells as automatically distinct is an invalid proof.

A verification condition is a mathematical implication whose validity establishes one proof obligation. For a loop with guard B and invariant I, the partial-correctness conditions are:

P⇒I,
{I∧B}C{I},
I∧¬B⇒Q.

Add obligations for a defined guard, safe body operations, termination of the body and a well-founded decrease. A failed verification condition may mean the program is wrong, but it may instead mean the annotation is too weak or unsuitable. For example, annotating while False with an invariant False fails initialization even though the command immediately terminates and leaves the state unchanged.

How to read the revised diagrams

A proof or arithmetic derivation advances through justified dependencies; formulas are native MathML. Bar height is value magnitude; stable labels identify records during moves and swaps. Place-value bits, quotient groups and arithmetic certificates expose the numeric representation. An indexed sorted strip exposes both half-open boundaries and their shrinking distance. Explicit subproblem/dependency edges expose splitting, evaluation and aggregation. Vertices, arrows and relation edges show actual membership, dependence or reachability.

Use the next-step control to inspect a completed transition. The caption states the assumptions and the exact state; a finite trace illustrates, but does not replace, the general proof. Record indices, logical boundaries, time coordinates and electrical polarity have distinct meanings.

Invariant discovery and termination

An invariant belongs to a specified checkpoint, normally just before the guard. Statements about the state halfway through the body may differ. To discover an invariant, rewrite the final goal as a relationship between processed data, unprocessed data and immutable inputs. Then add bounds sufficient to establish safety and an exit implication. Useful components include conservation laws, prefix properties, interval exclusion and snapshots of overwritten values.

Inductiveness is stronger than truth on reachable states. A predicate may hold at every reachable checkpoint but fail to be preserved at an unreachable state satisfying that predicate. Verification conditions quantify over all states allowed by the invariant; strengthening it can exclude those spurious states. Conversely, a transition-preserved predicate that is false initially tells us nothing about reachable states. The negation of an invariant is not automatically an invariant.

For total correctness, choose a variant in a well-founded set. A nonnegative integer V that strictly decreases on each executed body permits at most initial V iterations. The variant need not reach zero: the guard may become false sooner. A nonnegative real that decreases strictly can have an infinite sequence, such as 1,1/2,1/4,…. A nonnegative integer that merely never increases can also remain constant forever.

For nested progress, lexicographic pairs of nonnegative integers are useful. The pair (a,b) decreases if the first coordinate decreases, or if it stays equal and the second decreases. A decrease of a may reset b to any finite nonnegative value. Such a measure proves termination, but initial a+b need not bound the number of steps. If a program can nondeterministically reset b to arbitrarily large finite values, there may be no uniform step bound determined by the initial pair alone.

Counterexample discipline. To disprove a universal claim, give one admitted input, trace the relevant states, identify the failed obligation and state which hypothesis would repair it. Testing many inputs is evidence about those inputs. A proof establishes a quantified claim under its assumptions. Neither should be presented as the other.

Binary search with empty arrays and duplicate keys

The lower bound of a target t in a sorted array is the first index whose value is at least t, or n if no such value exists. This differs from finding an arbitrary equal element. Duplicates therefore belong to the contract, not to an optional afterthought.

def lower_bound(a, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if a[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

At the checkpoint, use these three clauses:

0≤lo≤hi≤n,
∀i<lo:A[i]<t,
∀i≥hi:A[i]≥t,

where the quantified indices are valid array indices. The unclassified interval is [lo,hi). Initialization holds because both classified ranges are empty. If lo<hi, floor midpoint selection gives lo≤mid<hi, so the access is safe.

If A[mid]<t, sortedness implies that every earlier array value is also less than t. Moving lo to mid+1 therefore classifies the entire discarded left region correctly. The old right classification remains unchanged. Otherwise A[mid]≥t, and sortedness makes every later value at least t; assigning hi=mid establishes the right classification.

Let L=hi-lo. The first branch produces L'=hi-mid-1; the second produces L'=mid-lo. Both lie between zero and ⌊L/2⌋. Hence L is a nonnegative integer variant and the loop terminates. At exit lo=hi, so the two classified regions exhaust the array. This proves the first eligible index, including the all-small case lo=n and the empty-array case lo=0.

For nonempty intervals the maximum number of body executions is ⌊log2n⌋+1, equivalently ⌈log2(n+1)⌉; an empty array requires zero. This counts body executions in this exact implementation, not arbitrary binary-search implementations. Depending on the target, some branches end sooner.

The tempting update lo = mid is wrong here. With A=[2] and t=3, it preserves the classification invariant but leaves the interval unchanged. Partial correctness cannot supply the missing termination argument. The midpoint expression also illustrates model dependence: lo + (hi-lo)//2 avoids adding the two endpoints, but the implementation still needs a type capable of representing the endpoints, their difference and all assigned values.

Sorting proofs that preserve records

Insertion sort: the saved-key hole

def insertion_sort(a):
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        key = a[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and a[j] > key:
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = key

At the outer checkpoint, the prefix A[0:i] is sorted and contains exactly the records initially in that prefix; the unprocessed suffix has not changed. The inner loop cannot use the assertion that the physical array remains a permutation after every assignment. A shift duplicates a value while the saved key temporarily lives outside the array. Instead regard position j+1 as a logical hole. The other prefix positions plus the saved key contain the original prefix multiset.

The portion left of the hole remains sorted. Every record shifted right has key strictly greater than the saved key, and its relative order with other shifted records is preserved. When the guard becomes false, either j=-1, or A[j]≤key. Filling the hole yields a sorted prefix of length i+1 and restores physical multiset equality. The inner variant is j+1 at a true guard; every shift decreases it by one. The outer loop has finitely many positions.

With tagged records (2,a),(1,b),(2,c), processing the last record with a strict greater-than comparison leaves (2,a) before (2,c). Replacing > by >= can move the newer equal-key record ahead of an older one. Sortedness and multiplicity survive, but stability does not. Comparison equality must be evaluated on keys, while assignments carry the full record.

Merge sort: two distinct inductions

To prove merge sort, first prove a merge lemma: given two sorted input sequences, merging them returns a sorted multiset union. At a merge checkpoint, the emitted prefix is sorted, every emitted value is no greater than each next available head, and the emitted prefix plus both unconsumed suffixes preserves the total input multiset. Consume the smaller head; consume the left head on equality when stable sorting is required. When one side is exhausted, append the remaining sorted suffix.

The merge variant is the number of unconsumed records across both inputs. Appending a tail can be viewed as repeated safe emissions. Array access requires testing exhaustion before comparing heads. A proof that assumes both heads exist cannot justify the final phase of the algorithm.

Now use strong induction on input length. Length zero or one is already sorted. For larger lengths, split into children of lengths ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉, both strictly smaller than n. The induction hypothesis proves both child contracts. The merge lemma proves the parent contract. The length measure proves recursive termination. The runtime recurrence is a separate analysis; solving a recurrence does not establish that the returned sequence has the right order.

Partitioning without skipping unclassified elements

For three-way partitioning around a pivot p, maintain four regions:

A[0:lt]<p,A[lt:i]=p,A[i:gt] unknown,A[gt:n]>p.

Here a relation on a slice means it holds for every value in that slice. The bounds are 0≤lt≤i≤gt≤n. Start with lt=i=0, gt=n, and repeat while i<gt.

def partition3(a, pivot):
    lt, i, gt = 0, 0, len(a)
    while i < gt:
        if a[i] < pivot:
            a[lt], a[i] = a[i], a[lt]
            lt += 1
            i += 1
        elif a[i] > pivot:
            gt -= 1
            a[i], a[gt] = a[gt], a[i]
        else:
            i += 1
    return lt, gt

In the less-than branch, when lt<i, the old element at lt belongs to the equal region, so moving it to the old scan position preserves the enlarged equal region. When lt=i, the swap is a self-swap and both boundaries advance together. In the greater-than branch, the incoming value from the old end of the unknown region remains unclassified. Advancing the scan index would skip it; keep i unchanged. The variant gt-i decreases by exactly one in all branches. Swaps preserve the multiset, and at termination no unknown element remains.

This procedure partitions; it does not sort either outer region. It is not stable in general. For arrays containing unordered values such as floating-point NaN, the three comparison cases may not have the assumed trichotomy. The exact ordered-key model must be stated.

Arithmetic algorithms and their domains

Division by repeated subtraction

For nonnegative integer X and positive integer Y, initialize q=0,r=X and repeatedly execute r = r - Y; q = q + 1 while r≥Y. The invariant is:

X=qY+r,q≥0,r≥0.

The body preserves conservation because (q+1)Y+(r-Y)=qY+r. The guard ensures the new remainder remains nonnegative. Since Y≥1, the variant r strictly decreases. At exit 0≤r<Y, which uniquely characterizes quotient and remainder. The number of body executions is ⌊X/Y⌋.

If Y=0, the conservation equality alone remains true and the guard stays true, but the remainder never decreases. If Y<0, the remainder grows under subtraction. Thus the positive-divisor assumption is a termination requirement and part of the mathematical division convention. Cambridge's worked partial-correctness derivation deliberately separates these obligations; it must not be read as a total-correctness proof for every divisor.

Euclid's algorithm

For integers a≥0,b≥0, use while b != 0: a,b = b,a % b, with simultaneous assignment. At each checkpoint,

gcd(a,b)=gcd(a0,b0)

and both variables remain nonnegative. Every common divisor of a,b divides a-qb, and every common divisor of b,a-qb divides a, so the gcd is preserved. Euclidean remainder gives 0≤amodb<b for a positive divisor. The old b is therefore a decreasing variant. At exit b=0, the gcd equals final a. Adopt the explicit convention gcd(0,0)=0 if that input is admitted.

Sequentially writing a=b; b=a%b destroys the old dividend: the second assignment now computes bmodb=0. A temporary variable or simultaneous assignment is essential. Bounds on division cost and exact bit complexity belong to runtime analysis, not to this gcd correctness proof.

Exponentiation by squaring

def power(x, y):
    assert y >= 0
    r, b, e = 1, x, y
    while e > 0:
        if e % 2 == 1:
            r *= b
        b *= b
        e //= 2
    return r

For exact integers and nonnegative exponent, use rbe=xy and e≥0, with immutable original x,y. In this algorithm the exponent-zero value is defined as one, including x=0. If old e=2k, the new product is r(b2)k=rb2k. If old e=2k+1, it is (rb)(b2)k=rb2k+1. The update of the accumulator must use the old base. At exit e=0, the invariant gives r=xy.

For positive e, floor halving strictly decreases it. For y>0, the number of loop iterations is ⌊log2y⌋+1; the number of accumulator multiplications is the population count of y in binary. This displayed implementation squares the base once per iteration, including the final iteration. An optimized implementation may avoid that last square without changing the result.

The unnecessary final square also matters to machine safety. With a signed 32-bit type, base 50,000 and exponent one, the mathematical result 50,000 is representable, but squaring the base creates 2,500,000,000, beyond the signed positive range. Thus representability of the final answer alone does not prove safety of every intermediate operation.

For modulus M≥1, reduce the initial base and each product modulo M, initialize r=1modM, and replace equality by congruence. The same even/odd proof establishes the residue. When M=1, the result is zero even for exponent zero. In a narrow machine type, multiplying two residues may overflow before reduction; modular algebra does not justify an unsafe intermediate product. Exact arithmetic, a sufficiently wide intermediate, or a proved overflow-safe modular multiplication routine is required.

Certificates and choosing a proof method

A certificate is additional information that lets a verifier check a claimed result. It need not reveal how the result was found. For sorting, check nondecreasing order and multiset preservation; checking only order accepts a constant array. A permutation of original record indices provides a direct witness that every input record appears exactly once. Its indices must be distinct, in range and consistent with the claimed output values.

For a finite weighted directed graph, a shortest-path certificate illustrates the difference between feasibility and optimality. Suppose all vertices under discussion are reachable from root s. Supply distances d, a parent chain ending at s for every other vertex, and d(s)=0. Each parent edge must exist and satisfy

d(v)=d(parent(v))+w(parent(v),v)

. Every graph edge must satisfy:

d(v)≤d(u)+w(u,v).

Summing these inequalities along any root-to-vertex path gives d(v) no greater than that path's weight. Summing the parent equalities gives an actual path of weight d(v). Together, they establish optimality. The parent relation must be acyclic and reach the root; a zero-weight cycle of parents supplies equalities but no root path. Negative edge weights do not invalidate this certificate argument, but a reachable negative cycle prevents a finite certificate satisfying all edge inequalities. Unreachable vertices require separate reachability and infinity conventions and are outside this finite-distance presentation.

For a rooted tree, structural induction is often simpler than a mutable-state invariant. For a recursive function, prove each child is smaller in a well-founded measure and use its complete contract, including preservation. For a greedy optimization algorithm, a local invariant can establish feasibility while optimality still requires an exchange or dominance argument. For dynamic programming, correctness requires an induction over the dependency order and proof that the recurrence covers every admissible decision. These are proof-method boundaries; the full greedy and dynamic-programming methods receive their own later chapters.

Claim Appropriate evidence Frequent invalid replacement
Exact output of an iterative procedure State invariant, exit implication and termination A runtime recurrence
Recursive correctness Base cases, smaller children and composition lemma A trace of one recursion tree
Optimality Feasibility plus an upper/lower bound meeting a witness Feasibility alone
Implementation safety Index, expression and arithmetic-domain checks Mathematical identities alone
Worst-case runtime Cost model, counted operations and bound Number of source-code lines

Authentic examination questions

Question 1. A recursive algorithm with reversed concatenation

Authentic examination · English translation

Phd CE 1405 · Q9 · PDF page 3. Independently derived solution; not an official key.

For an array of distinct values, SplitSort chooses its median m, recursively processes R={x:x>m} and L={x:x<m}, and returns concatenate(SplitSort(R), [m], SplitSort(L)); arrays of length at most one are returned unchanged. What is the output order?

1.

Descending up to the median, then ascending.

2.

Approximately random.

3.

Ascending.

4.

Descending.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

  1. The base cases of zero or one value are descending.
  2. Assume recursive outputs are descending. Every value in the first block is greater than m, and every value in the final block is less than m.
  3. Concatenating the descending greater block, m, and the descending smaller block therefore produces a descending whole array. Strong induction establishes the claim for every length.
  4. Median selection controls balance, not ascending direction. Option 1 misreads one recursive block; option 2 ignores determinism; option 3 would require left–median–right concatenation.

Transfer rule. Prove a recursion's semantic invariant separately from its running-time recurrence.

Concept model supporting this solution

This is a separate teaching example of Insertion sort: saved key and moving hole. Its numeric values are not the data or answer of this question. Use the stated invariant to interpret the written solution.

Question 2. Recursive reverse-stride copying

Authentic examination · English translation

MS CS 1393 · Q167 · PDF page 34. Independently derived solution; not an official key.

Copy every other element of an N -element array a, starting at its last element, into array b from index zero upward. Call store(N-1,0). Which pseudocode is correct? Syntax below treats parameters as integers and arrays as available in the procedure.

1.

if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

2.

if(n<0)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+1);

3.

if(n<0)return; b[i]=a[n]; store(n-2,i+2);

4.

if(n<0)return; b[i+1]=a[n]; store(n-1,i+2);

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. After t copies, the source index is N−1−2t and the destination index is t. The recursive edge must therefore decrease n by two and increase i by one.
  2. Option 1 starts at b[0], preserves those indices, and stops before a negative source index is read. It copies the ceiling of N/2 elements.
  3. All printed alternatives have the guard n<0. Option 2 starts writing at b[1]. Option 3 advances the destination by two and skips slots. Option 4 both starts at b[1] and uses a source stride of one, so it fails the requested selection.
  4. The source is integer pseudocode, not a strictly declared C17 interface. A real C implementation must use compatible signed bounds or a prechecked remaining-length representation.

Source correction. Options were visually rechecked against MSc CS 1393, Q167, PDF page 34 on 9 October 2026. The independently derived answer remains option 1. This is a bridge revisit, not a new unique archive question.

Question 3. Leaf weights in a binary tree

Authentic examination · English translation

Phd CE 1405 · Q3 · PDF page 2. Independently derived solution; not an official key.

For each leaf x at depth d of a binary tree T, put w(x)=2-d. If L is the set of all leaves and α=∑x∈Lw(x), which is always correct?

1.

α=1.

2.

α≤1.

3.

α>1.

4.

α<1.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Assign mass one to the root and half of a node's mass to each possible child. Missing children leave unused mass; a leaf receives exactly 2-d.
  2. Leaf masses are disjoint allocations of the root mass, so their sum is at most one. This can also be proved by structural induction on the two subtrees.
  3. Equality occurs in a finite full binary tree, including a single root leaf. A root with just one leaf child has sum one half, so equality is not guaranteed.
  4. These examples eliminate the always-equal and always-strict alternatives; the greater-than alternative contradicts conservation of mass.

Transfer rule. An upper bound can be universal even when equality depends on fullness of the structure.

Concept model supporting this solution

This is a separate teaching example of Lower bound: duplicate-aware interval elimination. Its numeric values are not the data or answer of this question. Use the stated invariant to interpret the written solution.

Question 4. Exact count of ordered triples

Authentic examination · English translation

Phd CS 1405 · Q20 · PDF page 8. Independently derived solution; not an official key.

Assume the variables have types large enough for the following code. What is the final value of Cod?

Cod = 10;
for (i = 1; i <= 15; i++)
  for (j = i; j <= 15; j++)
    for (k = j; k <= 15; k++)
      Cod++;
1.

610

2.

690

3.

630

4.

710

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Each increment corresponds to exactly one triple 1≤i≤j≤k≤15.
  2. Such triples are multisets of size three drawn from fifteen values, numbering
(15+3-13)=(173)=680

. 3. The initial value is ten, so the final value is 10+680=690. 4. Counting strictly increasing triples would give (153) and omit equal indices. Counting 153 would ignore the dependent bounds. All three other numeric options fail the exact multiset count.

Transfer rule. Weakly ordered loop indices correspond to combinations with repetition, and initialization is part of the output.

Question 5. Backward substitution through a quadratic

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Over exact integers, execute x = x + 3. What is the weakest precondition for final x2=25?

1.

x=5 or x=-5

2.

x=2 or x=-8

3.

x=8 or x=-2

4.
x=2
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Substitute the old expression into the final predicate: (x+3)2=25.

  2. Therefore x+3=5 or x+3=-5, giving x=2 or x=-8.

  3. Both inputs produce an allowed final square.

  4. Option 1 confuses final and initial values; option 3 reverses the shift; option 4 loses the negative branch.

  5. The word weakest requires every admitted solution, not one sufficient input.

  6. This calculation assumes exact arithmetic and a defined assignment.

Question 6. Sequence order changes the precondition

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Execute x=x+1; y=2*x; x=y-3 over integers. Which initial condition is weakest for final x=7?

1.
x=4
2.
x=5
3.
y=10
4.
x=10
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. Work backward.

  2. The final assignment requires old y-3=7, hence y=10.

  3. The middle assignment requires 2x=10.

  4. The first assignment then requires 2(x+1)=10, so initial x=4.

  5. Initial y is unconstrained because the middle statement overwrites it.

  6. A forward trace from four gives five, ten and seven, confirming the derivation.

  7. Option 2 omits the increment; option 3 constrains an overwritten value; option 4 mistakes an intermediate value for the input.

Question 7. Simultaneous versus sequential assignment

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Initially (x,y)=(5,8). Compare simultaneous (x,y)=(y,x+y) with sequential x=y; y=x+y. What are their respective results?

1.

(8,13) and (8,13)

2.

(8,16) and (8,13)

3.

(8,13) and (8,16)

4.

(5,13) and (8,16)

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. Simultaneous assignment evaluates both right sides in the old state, producing (8,5+8)=(8,13).

  2. Sequential execution first makes x=8; the second statement then uses that updated value and gives y=8+8=16.

  3. Option 1 ignores state change; option 2 exchanges the models; option 4 fails to assign the first coordinate.

  4. A temporary old value repairs the sequential Fibonacci update.

Question 8. Conditional weakest precondition

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived analogue: Cambridge conditional verification, PDF pages 52–53

For integer x, execute if x<0: x=-x; else: x=x+2. Which condition is weakest for final x≥3?

1.
x≠0
2.
x≥1
3.
x≤-3
4.

x≤-3 or x≥1

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

  1. In the negative branch, -x≥3 means x≤-3, which already implies the branch guard.

  2. In the nonnegative branch, x+2≥3 means x≥1.

  3. Combine the guarded branches by disjunction to obtain x≤-3 or x≥1.

  4. Inputs negative one and negative two refute option 1.

  5. Options 2 and 3 each omit one valid branch.

  6. The postcondition must be proved on both paths, including the otherwise branch.

Question 9. Which consequence direction is sound?

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

A known triple has precondition x≥0 and postcondition r=x2. Which replacement is always justified by consequence alone?

1.

Precondition true; postcondition r=x2

2.

Precondition x≥2; postcondition r≥0

3.

Precondition x≥0; postcondition r>x

4.

Precondition x<0; postcondition r≥0

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. The stronger precondition x≥2 implies x≥0, and the exact square postcondition implies r≥0 over real or integer values.

  2. Therefore option 2 follows.

  3. Option 1 expands the input domain; option 4 changes it to an unproved domain.

  4. Option 3 strengthens the output assertion and fails at x=0 or x=1.

  5. Consequence moves assumptions toward greater restriction and conclusions toward weaker requirements.

Question 10. Array aliasing is a logical condition

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived analogue: Cambridge array updates, PDF pages 19–22

Both indices are valid. Execute A[i]=1; A[j]=2. Which is the weakest condition on indices for final A[i]=1 and A[j]=2?

1.
i<j
2.
i>j
3.
i≠j
4.

No condition

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. If indices differ, the second write cannot change the first cell, so both desired values hold.

  2. If they coincide, the last write leaves that single cell equal to two, contradicting its required equality to one.

  3. Thus inequality is both necessary and sufficient.

  4. Either strict-order alternative is sufficient but not weakest because it excludes the opposite order.

  5. The no-condition alternative assumes separate array syntax means separate memory.

Question 11. Invariant strength can fail at an unreachable state

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original state-machine analogue informed by MIT §5.4

Start at (x,y)=(0,0) and repeatedly assign both coordinates simultaneously to (x+1,y+1). Is I:x≥0 by itself inductive under the transition, and is it sufficient to prove final x=y?

1.

Inductive and sufficient

2.

Inductive but insufficient

3.

Not inductive but sufficient

4.

Neither

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Every state with nonnegative x produces nonnegative x+1, so the predicate is inductive.

  2. However, it admits (3,8) and gives no relationship between the coordinates.

  3. Adding x=y yields a useful invariant and proves the equality at any termination checkpoint.

  4. Truth of a weak invariant does not supply an unrelated postcondition.

  5. The reachable states happen to satisfy equality, but the annotation must express it.

Question 12. Reachable truth need not be inductive

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original state-machine analogue informed by MIT §5.4

Start at x=0. The transition maps zero to zero and maps every positive x to -1. Which describes I:x≥0?

1.

False on a reachable state

2.

True on every reachable state but not inductive

3.

Inductive but false initially

4.

A proof that every state is reachable

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. The only reachable value is zero, because zero maps to itself.

  2. Thus the predicate holds on every reachable state.

  3. Yet the state x=1 satisfies the predicate and its successor -1 does not; this refutes preservation over all invariant states.

  4. Strengthening to x=0 removes the unreachable counterexample.

  5. Option 1 confuses possible integers with reachable ones, and option 3 reverses the failed obligation.

Question 13. A defective annotation does not condemn a program

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived analogue: Cambridge Exercise 45, PDF page 58

Annotate while False: x=0 with invariant False, initial assertion True, and final assertion True. Which claim is correct?

1.

The program diverges

2.

The final assertion is false

3.

Initialization of the chosen invariant fails, although the program is correct

4.

Every chosen invariant proves every loop

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. The loop executes zero bodies and terminates with the state unchanged, so the stated partial and total result is true.

  2. Nevertheless, initialization asks whether true implies false, which is invalid.

  3. A failed annotation can be repaired by using invariant true.

  4. This separates a proof artifact from program behavior.

  5. The preservation implication is vacuous here, but it cannot repair failed initialization.

Question 14. A loop with exact iteration count

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

For positive integer n, initialize x=n and execute while x>0: x=max(0,x-3). How many body executions occur?

1.
⌊n/3⌋
2.
⌈n/3⌉
3.
n
4.
⌈(n-1)/3⌉
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. After t bodies, x=max(0,n-3t).

  2. Termination first occurs when 3t≥n, whose smallest integer solution is ⌈n/3⌉.

  3. For n=1 the result is one, ruling out both floor and the fourth expression.

  4. The variant decreases by at least one at a true guard, but its initial value only gives a coarse upper bound; the exact state formula gives the precise count.

Question 15. Strict decrease over reals is insufficient

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original termination analogue informed by MIT §5.4

Start x=1 and repeat while x>0: x=x/2 in exact real arithmetic. Which is correct?

1.

The loop terminates after one step

2.

It terminates after finitely many steps because x decreases

3.

It does not terminate; nonnegative real strict descent is not well-founded

4.

It violates x≥0

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. After t steps, x=2-t>0 for every finite integer t, so the guard never becomes false.

  2. Strict decrease and nonnegativity hold throughout.

  3. A real measure therefore does not justify termination without an additional well-founded ordering or a fixed minimum decrease.

  4. Floating-point underflow would create a different execution model and must not be inserted into the exact-real problem.

Question 16. Lexicographic descent and step bounds

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original termination analogue informed by MIT §5.4

A nonnegative pair starts at (1,0). A step may replace it by (0,B) for any finite nonnegative integer B, after which the second coordinate decreases to zero. Which is true?

1.

Every execution terminates, but there is no uniform step bound from the initial pair alone

2.

Some execution has infinitely many decrements after the reset

3.

Every execution has at most one step

4.

The pair does not decrease lexicographically

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. The first step strictly decreases the first coordinate, so any finite reset is permitted by lexicographic descent.

  2. Thereafter exactly B unit decrements reach zero, making total length B+1.

  3. Each particular execution is finite, but choosing arbitrarily large finite B defeats any uniform bound depending only on the initial pair.

  4. Infinite reset values are not admitted.

  5. Option 4 wrongly applies componentwise ordering rather than lexicographic ordering.

3.

Midpoints (2,1,0); result one

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Four

Five

Six

Thirty-one

Question 19. A monotone invariant can coexist with nontermination

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

[2], target three

2.

[2], target one

[], target three

[2,4], target one

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. On the one-element interval [0,1), midpoint zero has value two below target three.

Question 20. Lower bound requires sortedness

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

It returns zero and is correct

It returns one; the duplicate rule failed

4.

It raises an index error

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  2. The next midpoint two has value three, so the upper boundary becomes two and the result is two.

  3. However, index zero already has value at least three.

  4. The step that discarded the left region relied on sortedness and is invalid for this input.

Question 22. A conditional interval bound

Question 24. The temporary array is not a permutation

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original refinement of Stanford insertion-sort proof

During insertion of key two into [1,4,2], after shifting four right and before restoring the key, the physical array is [1,4,4]. Which conservation statement is correct?

1.

The physical array alone preserves the input multiset

2.

Ignore the hole at index one and include the saved key two

3.

Ignore the last element and discard the key

4.

Only the sum of physical array values is preserved

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. After the shift, the logical hole is index one: that old value has moved right and its stale duplicate must not count twice.

  2. The other positions contain one and four; the external saved key is two.

  3. Their multiset is exactly the original prefix multiset.

  4. Filling the hole restores physical permutation.

  5. The physical sum changes from seven to nine, refuting option 4.

  6. A correct inner invariant accounts for temporary storage instead of demanding an assertion that the code does not preserve.

Question 25. Stability is independent of sortedness

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Insertion sort compares keys and moves entire records. If its inner comparison becomes a[j].key >= key.key, what happens to records (2,a),(2,b)?

1.

They remain in order (a,b)

2.

Their order becomes (b,a); sortedness and multiplicity still hold

3.

The keys become unsorted

4.

A record is lost

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. When inserting the second record, the equal first key satisfies the modified guard.

  2. The first record shifts right, and the saved second record fills index zero.

  3. The result is (2,b),(2,a), sorted by key and a permutation of the input but unstable.

  4. The example shows why proving only key order and multiset preservation does not establish stability.

  5. A strict greater-than shift preserves equal-key order.

    .

Question 27. Sorted output without preservation

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

A routine replaces every input entry by zero. Which verifier incorrectly accepts it as a sorting algorithm for arbitrary integer inputs?

1.

Check nondecreasing output only

2.

Check output multiset equals input multiset only

3.

Check both order and multiset

Check a bijection of record indices and ordered keys

Correct option: 1.

  2. For input [3,1], the multiset differs, and the other listed checks reject it.

Question 28. Recursive size must strictly decrease

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original boundary completion of Stanford recursive proof

A purported merge sort stops only at length one and splits length n into ⌊n/2⌋ and ⌈n/2⌉. What happens on an empty input?

2.

3.

It calls a child of size one

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  2. Both children again have length zero, so recursive calls reproduce the same unhandled size indefinitely.

  3. Correcting the base condition to length at most one covers empty input and makes both children strictly smaller for every remaining length.

  4. Runtime formulas derived only for positive sizes cannot repair a missing functional base case.

Question 34. A valid identity with an invalid termination proof

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived domain repair: Cambridge Exercise 53, PDF page 72

Use repeated subtraction with X=5,Y=0. Which statement explains the defect?

1.

The conservation identity fails initially

2.

The remainder becomes negative

3.

The invariant remains true, but the guard remains true and the remainder does not decrease

4.

The algorithm returns quotient zero and remainder five

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. Initialization gives 5=0·0+5.

  2. Every body leaves the remainder five while increasing the quotient, so conservation continues to hold.

  3. The guard tests 5≥0 forever.

  4. A nonnegative remainder that is merely constant is not a decreasing variant.

Question 35. Sequential updates in Euclid

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

With input (21,15), what does defective code while b!=0: a=b; b=a%b return, and what should correct Euclid return?

1.

Fifteen and three

2.

Three and three

3.

Six and fifteen

4.

Zero and three

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. The first statement overwrites the dividend with fifteen.

  2. The second uses the new dividend and computes 15mod15=0, so the defective loop returns fifteen.

  3. Correct simultaneous steps are

    (21,15)→(15,6)→(6,3)→(3,0)

    , returning three.

  4. The gcd invariant fails on the defective first step, because the old gcd is three but the new gcd is fifteen.

  5. Preserving old operands is essential.

Question 37. Power algorithm intermediate state

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived exponentiation analogue: CMU Contracts

For exact power(3,13), what is (r,b,e) after two complete loop bodies?

1.
(3,81,3)
2.
(9,81,3)
3.
(3,9,6)
4.
(81,3,3)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. Initially (1,3,13).

  2. The odd first body multiplies the accumulator by three, squares the base to nine and halves the exponent to six: (3,9,6).

  3. The even second body leaves the accumulator three, squares nine to 81 and halves six to three.

  4. The invariant checks 3·813=313.

  5. Option 3 is only the first checkpoint; option 2 incorrectly multiplies the accumulator on an even exponent.

Question 38. Two multiplication counts

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

For exponent 45, count accumulator multiplications and base squarings in the displayed exact power implementation.

1.

Six and four

2.

Four and six

3.

Five and five

4.

Four and five

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Binary 45 is 101101, with six bits and four one bits.

  2. The loop executes six bodies, squaring once per body; the accumulator multiplication executes only on the four odd-exponent checkpoints.

  3. The exact counts are therefore four and six.

  4. Avoid silently deleting the final square when analyzing this displayed code.

  5. An optimized version could have five squarings, corresponding to option 4 but not to this implementation.

Question 39. The old base matters

One

2.

Two

3.

Four

4.

Eight

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. The loop begins with base two and exponent one.

  2. Squaring first makes the base four.

  3. The odd branch then multiplies the accumulator one by four, and halving the exponent ends the loop.

  4. The result four differs from the required two.

  5. The even/odd invariant derivation uses the old base in the accumulator factor; changing execution order invalidates that derivation.

Question 40. Exponent zero and modulus one

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

2.

Accumulator 1modM

3.

Accumulator equal to the base

4.

Reject every exponent-zero input

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  2. With exponent zero no bodies execute, so the accumulator itself is returned.

Question 41. Reduction after overflow is too late

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Course-derived overflow extension: CMU Exercises 1–2

For eight-bit unsigned wrapping arithmetic, compute (200*200)%251 using an eight-bit wrapped product. Compare it with exact modular multiplication.

1.

Both are 91

2.

Wrapped result 64; exact result 91

3.

Wrapped result 91; exact result 64

4.

Both are 64

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Exact product is 40000.

  2. Modulo 256 it becomes 64 because 40000=156·256+64.

  3. Reducing that wrapped value modulo 251 still gives 64.

  4. Exact reduction gives 40000=159·251+91, hence 91.

  5. Wrapping modulo a power of two before reducing modulo a different modulus changes the arithmetic.

  6. A wide intermediate or an overflow-safe multiplication algorithm is required.

Question 42. Permutation index certificate

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

[1,0,2]
2.
[1,2,0]
3.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

Question 43. Meeting witness and bound proves optimum

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

In a minimization problem, a feasible solution has value 17, while a proved lower bound for every feasible solution is 17. What follows?

1.

The optimum is at most 17 only

2.

The optimum is at least 17 only

3.

The optimum equals 17

4.

The result depends on the search algorithm runtime

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. The feasible witness establishes optimum at most 17.

  2. The universal lower bound establishes optimum at least 17.

  3. Together they force equality.

  4. Feasibility alone would not exclude a cheaper solution, and the lower bound alone would not supply an attaining solution.

  5. Runtime is irrelevant to this logical certificate, although finding or checking the witness may have a cost.

Question 44. Distance edge inequalities are necessary

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original certificate problem

Graph edges are s→a of weight two, a→b of weight three, and s→b of weight four. Claimed distances are (0,2,5) with parent path through a. Which check detects failure?

1.

Parent path existence

2.

Root distance zero

3.

The edge inequality on s→b

4.

Nonnegative distances

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. The supplied parents give a real root-to- b path of weight five, so feasibility succeeds.

  2. But the direct edge gives d(b)≤d(s)+4, requiring 5≤4, which is false.

  3. There is a shorter path of weight four.

  4. Thus parent paths alone certify reachable distances, not shortest distances.

  5. This example isolates the optimality-bound component of the certificate.

Question 45. Parent cycles can pass local equalities

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original certificate counterexample

Graph edges are s→a of weight five, a→b of weight zero and b→a of weight zero. A certificate sets d(s)=d(a)=d(b)=0, and chooses parents parent(a)=b, parent(b)=a. What is missing?

1.

All edge inequalities already fail

2.

A requirement that parent chains reach the root

3.

The root distance must be five

4.

A requirement that weights be positive

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. All edge inequalities hold: zero is at most five on the root edge, and equal zero distances satisfy both zero edges.

  2. Both parent equalities also hold.

  3. Yet the parent cycle provides no path from the root attaining distance zero; the actual distances to the other vertices are five.

  4. Requiring every parent chain to end at the root excludes this false certificate.

  5. Strictly positive weights would be an unnecessary domain restriction rather than the general repair.

Question 46. Negative weights do not automatically defeat a certificate

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original certificate problem

Graph edges are s→a of weight four, s→b of weight five and a→b of weight negative three. Which distance assignment is certified by root-reaching parents and all edge inequalities?

1.
(0,4,5)
2.
(0,4,1)
3.
(0,1,4)
4.

No finite assignment because an edge is negative

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Choose parents of a and b as s and a.

  2. Parent sums give distances four and one.

  3. Edge checks are 4≤4, 1≤5 and 1≤4-3.

  4. Every parent chain reaches the root.

  5. Hence the certificate proves exact distances despite a negative edge.

  6. Option 1 violates the edge through a; option 3 cannot match its parent-path witness.

  7. Negative cycles, rather than every negative edge, are the relevant obstruction to finite shortest-path values in the reachable domain.

Question 47. A negative cycle contradicts finite labels

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original certificate problem

A reachable directed cycle has edge weights two, negative five and one. What do shortest-path edge inequalities imply when summed around the cycle?

1.

0≤-2, a contradiction

2.

0≤2, a proof of optimality

3.

d(s)=0 only

4.

A cycle is allowed whenever one edge is positive

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. Each inequality bounds the next distance by the previous distance plus its edge weight.

  2. Summing cancels every distance from both sides and requires zero at most total cycle weight 2-5+1=-2.

  3. This is impossible, so no finite assignment satisfying all cycle-edge inequalities exists.

  4. The contradiction depends on the negative total, not on which individual edges have which sign.

Question 48. Greedy feasibility is not optimality

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

For unweighted interval scheduling, choosing the earliest-start interval selects [0,10) and rejects [1,2),[2,3),[3,4). Which conclusion is justified?

1.

It is optimal because chosen intervals never overlap

2.

The output is feasible but may be suboptimal

3.

No greedy algorithm can be correct

4.

Endpoint conventions do not matter

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. The chosen singleton is feasible.

  2. Under half-open intervals, the three short intervals are mutually compatible and yield three selections instead of one.

  3. Therefore a non-overlap invariant proves feasibility but not maximal cardinality.

  4. An optimality proof needs an exchange or dominance argument for the chosen rule.

  5. This counterexample does not refute every greedy rule; earliest finish is a different rule.

  6. Endpoint conventions matter to whether adjacent intervals are compatible.

Question 49. Structural mass with missing children

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

A binary tree has leaves at depths one, two and three, with no other leaves. What is the leaf mass ∑2-d, and does it alone prove fullness?

1.

7/8; it does not prove fullness

2.

1; it proves fullness

3.

3/8; it proves fullness

4.

7/8; it proves fullness

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. The mass is 1/2+1/4+1/8=7/8.

  2. In a finite full binary tree root mass splits completely and all mass reaches leaves, so total mass is one.

  3. A mass below one means some possible child branches are missing.

  4. The given depths can occur in a tree with a chain containing missing branches.

Question 50. An accumulator formula for dependent loops

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

For integer n≥1, increment an accumulator once for each 1≤i≤j≤k≤n, starting from c0. What final formula follows?

1.
c0+(n3)
2.
c0+n3
3.
c0+(n+23)
4.
(n+23)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. Each weakly increasing triple corresponds to a multiset of size three drawn from n values.

  2. The count is (n+3-13)=(n+23).

  3. The accumulator invariant is initial value plus the number of already visited triples, yielding the displayed final formula.

  4. Strict-combination counting omits repeated indices; a cube ignores dependent bounds; the fourth option discards initialization.

Question 51. Recursion depth as an index invariant

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

Copy indices N-1,N-3,… from an input into consecutive output cells starting at zero. For N=10, what final copied source index and output length occur?

1.

Source zero; length five

2.

Source one; length five

3.

Source one; length six

4.

Source zero; length ten

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. The source indices are nine, seven, five, three and one.

  2. At depth t, the source is N-1-2t and destination is t.

  3. After five writes, the next source is negative one and recursion stops.

  4. Generally the output length is ⌈N/2⌉ and the last source is one for even positive lengths, zero for odd lengths.

  5. This state formula proves indexing and termination together.

Question 52. An exact invariant determines a nonlinear sum

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Course-derived summation analogue: Cambridge for-loop verification, PDF pages 57–58

Initialize s=0, k=1. While k<=n, execute s += 2*k-1; k += 1, with exact integers and n≥0. Which invariant at the checkpoint just before the guard is correct?

1.
s=k2
2.
s=(k-1)2
3.
s=2k-1
4.
s=n2
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Before iteration one, the sum is zero, equal to (1-1)2.

  2. If the invariant holds before k, adding 2k-1 gives (k-1)2+2k-1=k2, which is the required assertion before iteration k+1.

  3. At exit k=n+1, it yields s=n2.

  4. The empty range for n=0 leaves zero, agreeing with the formula.

  5. Option 1 places the assertion after the body rather than before it.

Question 53. An induction hypothesis must include preservation

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed hard

Original strengthening of Stanford recursive proof

For a recursive sorting proof, the induction hypothesis says only that each child output is sorted. Which additional assertion is essential to establish the complete parent sorting contract?

1.

The child runtime is linear

2.

Each child output preserves its input multiset

3.

The recursion tree is balanced

4.

Every input key is positive

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. Sorted child outputs could both be empty, satisfying the weak induction hypothesis while destroying all input records.

  2. Preservation of each child multiset plus preservation by merge proves preservation for the parent.

  3. Balance affects cost and strict size reduction affects termination, but neither implies value preservation.

  4. Positive keys are unnecessary because ordering works over any totally ordered key domain.

Question 54. A smallest counterexample to a weakened contract

Original/course-derived problem · author-assessed medium

Original problem

A claimed maximum routine initializes best=0 and scans a nonempty integer array using best=max(best,a[i]). Which input refutes its contract, and what invariant does the code actually maintain?

1.

[-2]; best is the maximum of zero and the processed values

2.

[2]; best is the minimum of processed values

3.

[0]; best is undefined

4.

[]; the input satisfies the nonempty precondition

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. For the admitted singleton negative two, the routine returns zero, which is not even an input value.

  2. Its genuine invariant is

    best=max(0,A[0],…,A[i-1])

    , so its logic solves a different problem unless inputs are constrained appropriately.

  3. Initializing with the first input value repairs the arbitrary-nonempty-integer contract.

  4. The empty array is outside that contract, so it cannot serve as the requested admitted counterexample.

  5. Writing the exact maintained invariant exposes the hidden assumption.

Complete summary and examination notes

What the contract actually claims

Rule 1

A precondition defines the admitted initial states. A counterexample outside that domain does not refute the stated contract, although it may reveal an unnecessarily narrow domain.

Rule 2

A postcondition must describe the required function, not merely a convenient property of its result. Sortedness alone accepts an empty or constant replacement array.

Rule 3

Partial correctness quantifies over normally terminating executions. It does not establish that an execution exists which terminates, or that an implementation is safe.

Rule 4

Total correctness adds termination for every admitted input. This chapter also checks safety explicitly, rather than allowing errors to escape a normal-termination specification.

Rule 5

An impossible precondition makes a partial-correctness triple vacuous. Check consistency before treating a successful logical derivation as a useful algorithm guarantee.

Rule 6

Immutable input snapshots distinguish original operands from evolving program variables. A power invariant uses original x,y and changing r,b,e.

Rule 7

Sortedness and multiset preservation are independent obligations. Stability and frame conditions are additional obligations when records and external memory matter.

Rule 8

A multiset records multiplicities. Set equality does not detect loss of a duplicate input record.

Rule 9

Mathematical exact integers, unsigned wrapping integers, signed machine integers and floating-point values have different semantics. Every formula is conditional on its declared model.

Rule 10

Signed C overflow is not ordinary modulo arithmetic. A modular proof must not be used to justify a signed-overflowing implementation.

Backward algebra and proof obligations

Rule 11

For a pure defined assignment, substitute the old expression into the postcondition:

wp(x:=E,Q)=Q[E/x]

. Do not assume the final variable value was already true initially.

Rule 12

For sequential commands, perform substitution in reverse execution order. Forward-order substitution can mix values from different checkpoints.

Rule 13

Simultaneous assignment evaluates all right sides in the same old state. Sequential assignment permits later right sides to observe earlier writes.

Rule 14

Backward substitution must avoid variable capture. Rename a bound variable when replacement would accidentally bind a formerly free occurrence.

Rule 15

A conditional proof covers the true branch under the guard and the false branch under its negation. An omitted else branch still contributes a skip obligation.

Rule 16

A stronger precondition implies the known precondition; a known postcondition implies a weaker replacement postcondition. Reversing either implication is unsound.

Rule 17

For array writes, equality of indices determines whether one write overwrites another. Valid indices do not imply distinct indices.

Rule 18

A loop proof checks initialization, body preservation and the exit implication. These establish partial functional correctness, not termination by themselves.

Rule 19

Guard evaluation and every access must be defined. A logically true invariant can still allow an invalid index or division by zero.

Rule 20

Verification conditions depend on the chosen annotation. A failed condition can indicate a bad annotation rather than a bad program.

Rule 21

A property of reachable states need not be inductive over all states satisfying that property. Add relationships that exclude unreachable spurious states when necessary.

Rule 22

Preservation without initialization gives no guarantee about reachable executions. A false initial invariant is not repaired by a vacuous preservation implication.

Rule 23

The negation of an invariant need not be invariant. A transition may enter the invariant region from outside it even though it never leaves that region from inside.

Termination, exact counts and boundaries

Rule 24

A nonnegative integer variant must decrease strictly at every executed body. Merely staying nonnegative or nonincreasing is insufficient.

Rule 25

A strictly decreasing nonnegative real can have infinitely many steps. Exact halving of a positive real is the standard counterexample.

Rule 26

A lexicographic pair can decrease while its second coordinate increases, provided its first coordinate decreases. Componentwise ordering is a different relation.

Rule 27

A well-founded proof establishes finiteness of each execution. It does not necessarily supply a uniform numeric bound under arbitrarily large nondeterministic resets.

Rule 28

A variant supplies an upper bound when each decrease is at least one. An exact state formula or a fixed decrease can yield a sharper exact count.

Rule 29

Recursive termination needs every invoked child's measure to be smaller. Correctness of base cases does not prevent a same-size recursive cycle.

Rule 30

Empty input often needs its own base case. “Stop at size one” is insufficient for a recursion that may receive size zero.

Rule 31

The number of guard evaluations can differ from the number of body executions by one. State which quantity an exact-count question asks for.

Rule 32

A counterexample should identify an admitted input, a failing state transition and the specific obligation that fails. A large random input is less informative than a minimal witness.

Searching, sorting and partitioning

Rule 33

Half-open lower bound searches [lo,hi) with 0≤lo≤hi≤n. The upper boundary may equal the array length without being a valid access index.

Rule 34

The lower-bound left classification is strictly below the target; its right classification is at least the target. These clauses determine the duplicate convention.

Rule 35

At a true guard, the floor midpoint satisfies lo≤mid<hi. This is the safety fact used before reading the midpoint element.

Rule 36

A below-target midpoint requires lo=mid+1. Keeping lo=mid can preserve classification while causing a one-element interval to repeat forever.

Rule 37

An eligible midpoint requires hi=mid, not mid-1, in this half-open implementation. Changing boundary conventions requires a fresh proof.

Rule 38

Sortedness justifies classifying the discarded region from a single midpoint comparison. Termination and valid indices do not establish correctness on unsorted input.

Rule 39

The maximum lower-bound body count is ⌊log2n⌋+1 for positive n, and zero for empty input. This count belongs to the displayed floor-midpoint implementation.

Rule 40

Upper bound replaces the classification by at most the target on the left and strictly greater on the right. Subtracting lower bound from upper bound counts target occurrences in a sorted array.

Rule 41

A safer midpoint formula avoids adding the endpoints, but its type must still represent the endpoints and their difference. Mathematical absence of overflow is not an automatic machine guarantee.

Rule 42

Insertion sort temporarily stores the key outside the array. Exclude the logical hole before asserting multiset preservation during shifts.

Rule 43

The strict greater-than insertion comparison preserves equal-key order. A greater-than-or-equal comparison can preserve sorting and multiplicity while breaking stability.

Rule 44

Insertion shifts correspond to strict inversions. Equal-key pairs do not require shifts in the stable implementation.

Rule 45

Merge correctness requires sorted output and preservation of both input multisets. It also requires an explicit exhausted-input case before reading a head.

Rule 46

Taking the left record on an equal-key merge preserves cross-half stability when both children are themselves stable.

Rule 47

A merge of nonempty lists of lengths p,q uses at most p+q-1 head comparisons in the standard implementation, because one list becomes exhausted before the final tail copy.

Rule 48

Merge-sort induction needs smaller child sizes, complete child contracts and a merge lemma. The runtime recurrence proves none of these functional claims on its own.

Rule 49

In three-way partition, the unknown region is [i,gt) and its length decreases exactly once per body. Therefore the displayed procedure executes exactly n bodies.

Rule 50

After swapping a greater-than-pivot value with the unknown region's last element, keep the scan index unchanged. The incoming value still needs classification.

Rule 51

A less-than-pivot swap may exchange with an equal-region value. The special case lt=i is a harmless self-swap with both boundaries advancing.

Rule 52

Three-way partition establishes three regions and preserves the record multiset. It does not establish stability or sorted outer regions.

Rule 53

Ordered-key proofs assume comparison trichotomy. Unordered floating-point NaNs require a separately specified comparison policy.

Arithmetic and certificates

Rule 54

Repeated subtraction uses X=qY+r with nonnegative quotient and remainder. The positive-divisor hypothesis supplies strict decrease and the usual remainder convention.

Rule 55

Conservation alone survives divisor zero. The zero-divisor loop demonstrates why a preserved identity cannot replace a termination proof.

Rule 56

Euclid preserves the gcd because common divisors are unchanged by replacing a dividend by its remainder. The positive current divisor supplies the strictly smaller remainder.

Rule 57

Euclid's operands must be updated using old values. Sequentially overwriting the dividend first usually returns the old divisor instead of the gcd.

Rule 58

If (0,0) is admitted, define its gcd convention explicitly. Avoid importing a positive-input proof into an unspecified edge case.

Rule 59

Exponentiation maintains rbe=xy at the guard checkpoint. Odd updates multiply by the old base, and even updates leave the accumulator unchanged.

Rule 60

Exponent zero executes no bodies. The chosen value is one in the exact implementation; a modular implementation must normalize it to 1modM.

Rule 61

For positive exponent y, the displayed power loop has bit-length many bodies and population-count many accumulator multiplications. It includes a final square that an optimized implementation may omit; this unused intermediate can overflow even when the final answer is representable.

Rule 62

Modular correctness uses congruence plus canonical output range. Congruence alone does not require returning the normalized residue.

Rule 63

Reduction after a narrow intermediate overflow can change the answer for a modulus different from the machine range. Prove the multiplication implementation as well as the modular identity.

Rule 64

An overflow check for nonnegative multiplication can compare an operand with a maximum-value quotient before multiplying, while handling a zero divisor in the check separately.

Rule 65

A sorting certificate needs ordered keys and a bijection to original records. An index list with a duplicate entry is not a permutation certificate.

Rule 66

A feasible minimization witness gives an upper bound on the optimum. A universal lower bound proves optimality only when it meets the witness value.

Rule 67

Shortest-path parent equalities establish path values only when every parent chain reaches the root. Local equalities can hold on a disconnected zero-weight parent cycle.

Rule 68

Edge inequalities give a lower bound on every path's weight after summation. Combined with an attaining parent path, they establish shortest-path optimality.

Rule 69

Negative edges do not invalidate the certificate proof. A reachable negative cycle contradicts finite edge inequalities when the cycle's inequalities are summed.

Rule 70

Unreachable vertices need separate reachability and infinity conventions. They are excluded from the finite-distance certificate model in this chapter.

Rule 71

Structural induction suits recursive tree properties, including conserved leaf mass. Missing child branches explain why a universal bound need not be an equality.

Rule 72

A feasibility invariant is insufficient to prove a greedy choice optimal. Supply an exchange, dominance or matching-bound argument for the specific objective.

Rule 73

Dynamic-programming correctness requires a recurrence covering all legal choices and an acyclic dependency order. A table of plausible values is not a proof.

Rule 74

Finite exhaustive tests can decisively refute a claim and verify a bounded domain. They cannot establish an unbounded theorem or guarantee every unseen examination answer.

A complete procedure for a new examination problem

Read the input domain and arithmetic model first. Identify the requested quantity: output, correctness, safety, termination, stability or cost. Write the state at the checkpoint and an invariant connecting it to the original input. Verify initialization, each branch and the exit implication. If termination is relevant, give a well-founded decreasing measure. For an exact count, derive the number of transitions rather than quoting a complexity class. Check empty, singleton, duplicate, zero and exceptional-parameter cases permitted by the problem. Finally, refute distractors with either the derived formula or a concrete admitted counterexample. This procedure supports reasoning across implementations; it is not a promise that every unfamiliar problem will yield to a memorized template.

Binary-search proof laboratory

The laboratory shows every checkpoint, the unresolved interval, the classified regions and the termination measure. Compare the correct update with a deliberately faulty update on a one-element interval. A reported counterexample refutes that implementation; bounded examples do not replace the general proof above. The laboratory admits only sorted integer inputs within an exact, bounded arithmetic range.

Use zero through 24 sorted integers between negative 999 and 999. The target uses the same range. A repeated nonempty interval is reported as a stalling counterexample; the demonstration stops safely after detecting that repetition.
